In Chapter 14 we introduced the independent-samples ANOVA for use with between-participants designs. In this chapter we'll introduce another variant, the related-samples ANOVA. Conceptually, there's really nothing new here. Just like the related-samples $t$ test, this is for use with within-participants or matched-subjects designs. We'll just need to examine some of the new sources of variance that we can partition differently here by virtue of the related-samples design.

## Same numbers, different analysis

To recap the idea of these different designs, the independent-samples ANOVA we used in the previous lecture is for use with between-participants designs in which each sample consists of different people and therefore independent observations. Like I mentioned, because we have different participants in each treatment group, any between-groups variability could either be due to a treatment effect or any individual differences between participants. Again, we might happen to end up with groups with slightly different compositions just by chance alone. With this abstract diagram I first introduced with the related-samples $t$ test, I genuinely used a random sampling procedure to generate these groups of dots. And each group has a slightly different composition of colors. There's no real systematic difference between the groups. There's no treatment effect — only the slightly different aggregations of different individuals.

With a repeated-measures design or a matched-samples design, each group is made up of the same people or people we deliberately paired up to be similar on any variable or variables we think are important. And the primary advantage of these designs is that we rule out those kinds of individual differences as a potential source of variability between groups.

By eliminating that source of variability, we produce a more powerful test statistic. Like we said when we first introduced this idea, another advantage of repeated-samples designs, though not matched-samples designs, is that we require fewer participants. Everyone contributes data to all treatment conditions. With three conditions we only need a third of the participants compared to an independent-samples design, so this can be a big practical benefit. But remember, there are disadvantages as well. We're assuming that people haven't changed in any important way between treatments, but maybe they have. There could be order effects, improvement through practice, some change due to world events, or natural improvement in people's symptoms.

## Partitioning variance in related samples

<!-- FIX: "cancel(ed) out" here and in tutorial steps 1 and 4 contradicts Chapter 14, which replaced that story: each mean square estimates the same variance, and a treatment effect inflates only the numerator. Also align "sampling error and individual differences" with Chapter 14's "chance". -->

So let's think about this in terms of partitioning the variance in the data. Let's start by recapping this procedure for independent-samples designs again. There is the total variability in the data. We can partition that into the variance, or mean square, between groups and variance within groups.

So what contributes to those different types of variability? Any treatment effect only contributes to variability between groups, not within. In Chapter 14 I simplified a little by saying that chance also contributes to differences between groups. But here we can be more specific. That kind of chance difference consists both of sampling error, the general discrepancy between statistics and parameters, and individual differences, the fact that some people score higher or lower than others because of their abilities or traits or preferences or whatever. And both sampling error and individual differences contribute to variance within groups as well.

So conceptually, to be more specific about things, the independent-samples $F$ ratio equation consists of the treatment effect, sampling error, and individual differences in the numerator, and sampling error and individual differences in the denominator. So the error and individual differences are sort of canceled out by the ratio, quantifying whatever treatment effect is above and beyond those chance differences.

### Removing individual differences

<!-- FIX: "error variance consists only of sampling error" isn't right. The residual also includes people responding differently to the conditions (person × condition variability). -->
<!-- FIX: section partly repeats the callout above it. Trim once the prose is revised. -->

With the related-samples ANOVA, we start out the same, partitioning the total variance into variance between groups and variance within groups. Any treatment effect still contributes to variance between groups and not within groups. Sampling error still contributes to both differences between and within groups. But like I said, individual differences are eliminated as a potential source of variability between groups by virtue of the design — it's the same people or matched subjects in each group. So the individuals do not differ between groups. But of course, they do still differ within groups. So individual differences are a potential source of within-group variance.

So if we use the same numerator and denominator here as for the independent-samples ANOVA, the ratio wouldn't be balanced anymore. We'd have treatment plus error in the numerator and error plus individual differences in the denominator. So those different sources of variability would contribute differently to the numerator and denominator and wouldn't cancel out nicely in the ratio like they did before.

This would be a problem. And so with related samples, we have a little extra work to do, because, happily, we can partition out the variance in the denominator, separating the sampling error and the individual differences. We will partition that within-group variance into two components: error variance, labeled $MS_{\text{error}}$, and between-people variance, $MS_{\text{people}}$. As the name suggests, the error variance consists only of sampling error and the between-people variance consists only of the individual differences. We'll see how exactly we're able to quantify these different sources in a moment.

### The modified $F$ ratio

We will still use the same numerator, $MS_{\text{between}}$, but we're going to use a different denominator for the $F$ ratio: $MS_{\text{error}}$. So conceptually, the balance is restored to our equation. The individual differences are removed from the numerator simply by virtue of the design. And now we've removed them from the denominator by partitioning out the individual differences. Our ratio consists of any treatment effect plus sampling error in the numerator, and sampling error alone in the denominator. Now, as before, the ratio effectively cancels out the error, quantifying any treatment effect.

## Sums of squares and degrees of freedom

So here's how we calculate this modified $F$ ratio for related-samples data. We start with the sums of squares and degrees of freedom. And the total, between-groups, and within-groups components are exactly the same as they were for the independent-samples designs.

Then we get to the two new components for between-people and error variability. The equation[^related-computational] for between people has the same form as $SS_{\text{between}}$, with person means in place of group means:

$$ SS_{\text{people}} = \Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 $$

$M_{\text{person}}$ is the mean of one person's scores across the conditions. Remember, for the between-groups variability, the equation sums the squared deviation of each group mean from the grand mean, with each one multiplied by the number of scores that mean represents. For between-people variability, the idea is the same, but instead of averaging scores for each group we average them for each person. Then we find the squared deviation of each person's mean from the grand mean, and multiply by $k$, the number of conditions, since each person's mean represents $k$ scores.

The final component, and the one that will become our denominator, is what's left. Anything left over after taking the individual-difference variability out of within-groups variability is the error variability, so we can find it by subtraction:

$$ SS_{\text{error}} = SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}} $$

Or we can get the same answer directly, from each score's deviation from its group mean once that person's overall deviation from the grand mean has been taken out: $SS_{\text{error}} = \Sigma (X - M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{group}} + M_{\text{grand}})^2$.

The two new components have degrees of freedom of their own. For $SS_{\text{people}}$, we computed the deviation of each person's mean from the grand mean. So that's $n$ means, deviating from a single grand mean, and $df_{\text{people}} = n - 1$, the number of people minus one. (Since everyone contributes one score to each condition, $n$ is also the number of scores in each condition.) The error degrees of freedom are what's left of $df_{\text{within}}$:

$$ df_{\text{error}} = df_{\text{within}} - df_{\text{people}} = (N - k) - (n - 1) = (k - 1)(n - 1) $$

It's worth taking the time to really understand these equations on a conceptual level. It should hopefully make more sense when we work through an example a little bit later.

[^related-computational]: As in Chapter 14, there's also a computational version of this formula. It uses $P$, a participant total (the sum of the scores for one person), and $G$, the grand total.

    $$ SS_{\text{people}} = \Sigma \frac{P^2}{k} - \frac{G^2}{N} $$

    We'll stick with the definitional formula here too.

### Mean squares and $F$

<!-- FIX: "making this a more powerful statistic" isn't guaranteed: $df_{\text{error}}$ drops, as Chapter 13 says for $t$. -->

Once we calculate the required sums of squares and degrees of freedom, the rest is easy. We calculate the variances for the numerator and denominator, $MS_{\text{between}}$ and $MS_{\text{error}}$, by dividing the relevant sums of squares by degrees of freedom. And then we calculate the $F$ ratio by dividing the numerator by the denominator. Again, the numerator is exactly the same we would have used for an independent-samples design, $MS_{\text{between}}$. We just have to remember to use the different denominator here, $MS_{\text{error}}$.

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{between}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}} \\
MS_{\text{error}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}}
\end{align}
$$

$$ F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}} $$

And the interpretation of the $F$ ratio is exactly the same. The greater than 1 our $F$ ratio is, the more of a treatment effect there appears to be over and above sampling error. And because the denominator excludes an additional source of variability here, it will be smaller, making this a more powerful statistic than the regular independent-samples version.

## A related-samples ANOVA, step by step

<!-- DATA notes: from Triplett's Table I, trials 1-3, rounded as in Chapter 13. Race first = group A (later alone is trial 3, competition trial 2). Alone first = group B (later alone is trial 2, competition trial 3). Violet and Howard are Chapter 13's kids, with the same Alone and Competition times. People are 93% of SS_within. Ignoring the pairs: F(2, 15) = 1.94, p = .178, critical 3.68. Eta squared = .21. -->

So we'll run through a hypothesis test using a related-samples design. We'll use Triplett's data again, with six children from one of his tables and three conditions: their first race alone, a later race alone, and a race in competition. @tbl-related-anova-data shows the data.

| Child | Order | First alone | Later alone | Competition |
|:------|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Violet F. | Race first | 54 | 45 | 43 |
| Howard C. | Race first | 42 | 39 | 36 |
| Inez K. | Race first | 37 | 36 | 35 |
| Mary W. | Alone first | 56 | 53 | 46 |
| Bertha A. | Alone first | 56 | 49 | 48 |
| Lucile W. | Alone first | 52 | 50 | 43 |
| $M$ | | 49.50 | 45.33 | 41.83 |
| $SS$ | | 323.50 | 221.33 | 138.83 |

: Times (in seconds) for six children from Triplett's study, in three conditions. {#tbl-related-anova-data}

Each row represents a single child who did all three races. So instead of comparing independent samples we're comparing related samples, looking at the variability among each child's own performance in the three different conditions. So obviously here we'll use the related-samples ANOVA procedure.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

As always, we start that hypothesis test by stating our hypotheses. Again, the null here is that all three populations from which we've created these samples have identical means — that $\mu_{\text{first alone}} = \mu_{\text{later alone}} = \mu_{\text{competition}}$. The alternative hypothesis is that at least one condition differs from at least one other.

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

Step two is to determine the critical value for the test, with $\alpha = .05$. And we do so using the same table as before. The only difference is that we need to be aware of the different degrees of freedom for the different denominator. The numerator is the same as before; $df_{\text{between}}$ is $k$, the number of conditions, minus one. We have three conditions, so the degrees of freedom for the numerator here is 2.

The degrees of freedom for the new denominator, $df_{\text{error}}$, is $df_{\text{within}}$ minus $df_{\text{people}}$, so $N - k$ for degrees of freedom within, minus $n - 1$, the number of people minus one. So here that works out to $18 - 3 = 15$, minus $6 - 1 = 5$. Fifteen minus five gives us ten. In @tbl-related-anova-critical, the column for 2 and the row for 10 give a critical $F$ of 4.10.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-critical}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaCriticalTable makeFTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the competition test","alpha":0.05,"df1":{"from":1,"to":4},"df2":{"from":8,"to":12},"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"df1":2,"df2":10,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="F table excerpt for numerator df 1 through 4 and denominator df 8 through 12, highlighting the .05 critical value of 4.10 at F(2, 10)." >}}

An excerpt of the $F$ table, with the critical value for $df = 2$ and $10$ highlighted.
:::

And like I mentioned when we introduced the related-samples $t$ test, notice that we require a more extreme critical value to reject the null hypothesis than the 3.68 we'd need for $F(2, 15)$, because of the lower degrees of freedom. But we should have a more powerful test statistic because of the elimination of individual-differences variability.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-degrees-of-freedom.qmd >}}

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Step three is to calculate the $F$ ratio for the data. Like the calculations for the independent-samples ANOVA, this is a little labor intensive. But it's worth practicing to make sure you understand how to use each equation and what each component represents.

It's a good idea to use a summary table as you work through this by hand. It's the same as we used in Chapter 14; it just has additional rows for new sources of variance: between people and error. @tbl-related-anova-summary-blank shows the equations for each element.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-summary-blank .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Between groups | $\Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k - 1$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}}$ | $\dfrac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}}$ |
| Within groups | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2$ | $N - k$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Between people | $\Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $n - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Error | $SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}}$ | $(k - 1)(n - 1)$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}}$ | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $N - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

A related-samples ANOVA summary table, showing each equation.
:::

To save you some trouble, I've already worked on some of what you'll need. @tbl-related-anova-data has each condition's mean and sum of squares. And for convenience, here are $n$, $k$, $N$, and $M_{\text{grand}}$. Even though I'm giving you these, it's important to make sure you understand how I arrived at each one. It would be a good idea for you to calculate them yourself, to double check my work and check your understanding.

$$n = 6 \qquad k = 3 \qquad N = 18 \qquad M_{\text{grand}} = 45.56$$

The only new calculation is $SS_{\text{people}}$. @tbl-related-anova-people lays it out, starting from each child's mean across the three conditions. (I've rounded the values I'm showing to two decimal places, but the calculations use the unrounded values, so you'll need to do the same if you want your answers to match mine exactly.)

| Child | $M_{\text{person}}$ | Deviation | Squared, times $k$ |
|:------|--:|--:|--:|
| Violet F. | 47.33 | 1.78 | 9.48 |
| Howard C. | 39.00 | $-6.56$ | 128.93 |
| Inez K. | 36.00 | $-9.56$ | 273.93 |
| Mary W. | 51.67 | 6.11 | 112.04 |
| Bertha A. | 51.00 | 5.44 | 88.93 |
| Lucile W. | 48.33 | 2.78 | 23.15 |
| $SS_{\text{people}}$ | | | **636.44** |

: Each child's mean, its deviation from the grand mean, and that squared deviation counted once per condition ($k = 3$). Values are rounded; the sum uses unrounded values. {#tbl-related-anova-people}

So remember, you'll need to calculate the sums of squares, degrees of freedom, mean squares, and $F$ ratio.

Here's the full working, so you can check your answers:

$$
\begin{align}
SS_{\text{total}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2 = 860.44 \\
SS_{\text{within}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2 \\ &= 323.50 + 221.33 + 138.83 = 683.67 \\
SS_{\text{between}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\ &= 6(3.94)^2 + 6(-0.22)^2 + 6(-3.72)^2 = 176.78 \\
SS_{\text{people}} &= \Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\ &= 9.48 + 128.93 + 273.93 + 112.04 + 88.93 + 23.15 = 636.44 \\
SS_{\text{error}} &= SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}} = 683.67 - 636.44 = 47.22
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
df_{\text{total}} &= N - 1 = 18 - 1 = 17 \\
df_{\text{within}} &= N - k = 18 - 3 = 15 \\
df_{\text{between}} &= k - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2 \\
df_{\text{people}} &= n - 1 = 6 - 1 = 5 \\
df_{\text{error}} &= (k - 1)(n - 1) = (3 - 1)(6 - 1) = 10
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{between}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}} = \frac{176.78}{2} = 88.39 \\
MS_{\text{error}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}} = \frac{47.22}{10} = 4.72
\end{align}
$$

$$ F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}} = \frac{88.39}{4.72} \approx 18.72 $$

And here's the completed summary table:

::: {#tbl-related-anova-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Between groups | 176.78 | 2 | 88.39 | 18.72 |
| Within groups | 683.67 | 15 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Between people | 636.44 | 5 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Error | 47.22 | 10 | 4.72 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 860.44 | 17 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Completed related-samples ANOVA summary table for the competition example.
:::

### Step 4: Make a decision

So now we've calculated our $F$ ratio, we're ready to make our decision. We compare it to the critical value we figured out from the table, and if our $F$ ratio is bigger than the critical value, we reject the null hypothesis. So here with our $F$ of 18.72, well beyond the critical value of 4.10, we can comfortably reject the null. There is a significant difference among our three conditions. The corresponding $p$-value is about $.0004$, so $p$ is less than $\alpha$.

::: {#fig-related-anova-decision}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"f","df1":2,"df2":10,"title":"Null distribution: F(2, 10)","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[0,20],"xTicks":6,"labels":{"x":"F ratio"},"shade":{"tail":"right","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":4.102821,"label":"4.10","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":18.717647,"label":"F = 18.72","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null F distribution with 2 and 10 degrees of freedom. The rejection region lies above 4.10; the observed F of 18.72 is far into the rejection region." >}}

The observed $F = 18.72$ falls beyond the critical value of the null $F$ distribution with $df = 2$ and $10$.
:::

### Step 5: Estimate the effect, compare the conditions, and consider power

#### Effect size: partial $\eta^2$

<!-- FIX: Chapter 14 reports effect size whether or not the test is significant. "Partial" should be explained against Chapter 14's bucket: a share of what's left once people are set aside. -->

Since we have a significant difference, we next need to determine the effect size. In Chapter 14 we used $\eta^2$. Here we use a slightly different version called partial eta squared, $\eta^2_p$. Rather than just the $SS_{\text{total}}$ for the denominator, it uses $SS_{\text{total}} - SS_{\text{people}}$. That's because we don't have individual differences in the numerator, the $SS_{\text{between}}$, and so we want to get rid of them in the denominator as well. So we call it $\eta^2$ partial to acknowledge that we're quantifying the variability between groups as a proportion of the partial rather than the total variability in the data. An equivalent form we could put the denominator in is $SS_{\text{between}} + SS_{\text{error}}$. And if you understand why that's the same as $SS_{\text{total}} - SS_{\text{people}}$, that's a good indication that you're grasping this idea of partitioning variance. So here we get an answer of $.79$:

$$\eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{SS_{\text{total}} - SS_{\text{people}}} = \frac{176.78}{860.44 - 636.44} = .79$$

#### Post-hoc tests

<!-- FIX: the experiment-wise paragraph below repeats Chapter 14. One sentence is enough. -->

Since the ANOVA revealed a significant difference, is to conduct post-hoc tests to determine where exactly the difference is — which conditions are different from which others. Again, we use the Tukey's HSD equation. First, we have to find the appropriate studentized range statistic, $q$, from a table. It depends on the number of means we're comparing and the degrees of freedom for the denominator of the $F$ ratio. So with three conditions and degrees of freedom of ten, $q$ is 3.88.

We then use that value in this equation, multiplying it by the square root of the denominator of the $F$ ratio divided by $n$, the number of scores per condition. Here we get an answer of 3.44, meaning that any difference between group means of more than 3.44 seconds will be a significant difference at the $.05$ level.

$$HSD = q \sqrt{\frac{MS_{\text{error}}}{n}} = 3.88 \sqrt{\frac{4.72}{6}} = 3.44$$

| Comparison | Absolute difference | Exceeds 3.44 seconds? |
|:--|--:|:--:|
| First alone vs. later alone | 4.17 seconds | Yes |
| Later alone vs. competition | 3.50 seconds | Yes |
| First alone vs. competition | 7.67 seconds | Yes |

And remember, the whole point of doing these post-hoc tests is that we are maintaining our experimentwise alpha at $.05$, even though we're making multiple comparisons, whereas if we just did a bunch of $t$ tests, each with its own alpha of $.05$, we'd end up with a much larger experimentwise alpha rate, meaning a larger chance of having made a Type I false positive error somewhere.

#### Statistical power

## Reporting and interpreting results

So finally, we're ready to report the results and call it a day. As usual, you need descriptives for each condition; a statement of what test was performed and whether it was significant; the test statistic itself with degrees of freedom; $p$ compared to $\alpha$; and effect size. And here we include a summary of the post-hoc tests stating which conditions differed significantly and nonsignificantly.

> In this selected six-child example, a single-factor, related-samples ANOVA revealed a significant difference among children's times on their first race alone ($M = 49.50$, $SD = 8.04$ seconds), a later race alone ($M = 45.33$, $SD = 6.65$ seconds), and a race in competition ($M = 41.83$, $SD = 5.27$ seconds); $F(2, 10) = 18.72$, $p < .001$, $\eta^2_p = .79$. Tukey HSD comparisons indicated that all three conditions differed significantly: children were faster on the later race alone than the first, and faster still in competition.
